content: The use of prothionamide or ethionamide in the treatment of multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) should only be considered for patients on longer treatment regimens if more effective drugs such as bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid are unavailable, or if no better options exist to construct an effective regimen. This recommendation is conditional, with very low certainty regarding the effectiveness of these drugs. Similarly, para-aminosalicylic acid may be included in longer MDR/RR-TB regimens under the same conditions and limitations. However, clavulanic acid is strongly discouraged for use in MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens due to low certainty of its effectiveness. A treatment regimen lasting 6–9 months, composed of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), may be used under operational research conditions for MDR-TB patients with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. This applies to patients aged 14 years and older who have not been previously exposed to bedaquiline and linezolid or have been exposed for no more than two weeks. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low certainty of evidence. Imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem are administered with clavulanic acid, which is only available in combination with amoxicillin. However, amoxicillin-clavulanic acid is not considered an additional effective TB agent and should not be used without imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem. For monitoring the response to MDR/RR-TB treatment in patients on longer regimens, sputum culture is recommended in addition to sputum smear microscopy. Monthly repetition of sputum culture is desirable. This recommendation is strong, with moderate certainty regarding the accuracy of these tests. In children under 15 years of age, who often cannot produce sufficient sputum for bacteriological diagnosis, culture may be more sensitive in detecting viable TB bacilli, even when present in very low quantities. For children unable to expectorate, gastric aspirates or induced sputum may be alternatives, though frequent repetition of these tests may not be feasible. Decentralized and family-centered, integrated models of care are recommended to improve TB case detection and the provision of tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) in children and adolescents. These approaches aim to address gaps in TB care by integrating services into primary healthcare (PHC) and community settings, ensuring that care is accessible and family-focused. Decentralization should prioritize areas with poor access to existing services or high TB prevalence. Family-centered care involves household-level interventions to identify individuals needing TB evaluation, TPT, or treatment support. The implementation of decentralized and family-centered care requires adequate training of healthcare workers, investment in infrastructure, and integration of TB services into general PHC. Active contact investigation at the community and household levels is critical for enhancing case detection and TPT provision. Task shifting, which involves training all healthcare providers in recognizing and managing TB, is an important factor in successful implementation. Adolescents with TB often present similarly to adults and may require different interventions than younger children. TPT provision has historically focused on children under five years of age, but target groups have expanded to include contacts of all ages. Integration of TB services into care for children with overlapping illnesses, such as severe acute malnutrition, pneumonia, or HIV, can improve case detection and TPT coverage. Family-centered care emphasizes the involvement of families in TB management, including education on recognizing TB symptoms, understanding the importance of contact history, and reducing stigma. High-yield entry points for TB care include malnutrition clinics, antenatal care, immunization programs, and general pediatric clinics. Overall, decentralized and family-centered approaches are considered feasible and cost-effective, with potential to improve equity and program success. However, initial investments in infrastructure, training, and community engagement are critical for effective implementation.
